The claim flags it as 'elsewhere', so it is uncited rather than miscited, but it currently rests on no source and needs one. Byline confirmed: Amy Gentry, LoneStarCon 3.

claims.feature: thematic core: the heart in conflict
claims.claim: Martin quotes Faulkner that the only thing worth writing about is the human heart in conflict with itself, which drives his interior POV.
claims.quote: the human heart in conflict with itself

verdict.trueWording: The only thing worth writing about is the human heart in conflict with itself.
verdict.note: Verbatim, and Martin explicitly frames it as his credo: "My credo as a writer has always been Faulkner's Nobel Prize acceptance speech where he said..." One overreach: 'which drives his interior POV' is the claimant's inference — on this page Martin invokes Faulkner to argue that magic must never be the solution to the problem, not to explain viewpoint.

claims.claim: Martin cites the Iliad as a model where the hero of one side is the villain of the other, shaping his multi-sided viewpoint scheme.
claims.quote: The hero of one side is the villain

verdict.trueWording: The hero of one side is the villain of the other side.
verdict.note: Verbatim, and the Iliad attribution is explicit: "I've been always very impressed by Homer and his Iliad, especially the scene of the fight between Achilles and Hector. Who is the hero and who is the villain?" Caveat: 'shaping his multi-sided viewpoint scheme' is inference — this answer is about grey characters, and Martin's POV-technique answer is a separate question earlier in the same interview.

claims.claim: The same reviewer finds the sex scenes reliant on clichés such as 'drunk with desire'.
claims.source: The Erstwhile Philistine, 'The Literary Crimes of George R.R. Martin' (2012-03-21)
claims.quote: drunk with desire

verdict.trueWording: someone being drunk with desire for the other person
verdict.note: Quote verbatim inside 'They usually involve someone being drunk with desire for the other person, their head swimming with the wine of lust or some such nonsense.' Caveat: 'cliche' is the summarizer's word, not the author's — he writes 'clunky to the extreme' and 'the obligatory mention of naughty body parts'; 'cliches' appears only in reader comments.

claims.claim: Commenters on that essay counter that Martin has a penchant for pseudo-archaic language and, once he likes a term ('much and more', 'leal'), uses it everywhere.
claims.quote: GRRM has a penchant for pseudo-archaic language

verdict.trueWording: I think GRRM has a penchant for pseudo-archaic language
verdict.note: Verbatim in the comment by 'Wenyip' (Aug 17 2011), which also names 'much and more' (and 'little and less') and cautions against reading much into 'leal'. Minor: it is one commenter, not 'commenters' plural, and the tone is a caveat rather than a counter-argument.

claims.claim: A lexicographer notes 'ser', 'southron' and 'craven' are 15th-century forms and 'turncloak' is Martin's coinage from 'turncoat'.

verdict.trueWording: date from 1451, 1488, and 1400 respectively
verdict.note: No quote field to check. Page: 'Ser for Sir, Southron for Southern, and craven meaning cowardly all date from 1451, 1488, and 1400 respectively, according to the Oxford English Dictionary' and 'turncloak, which is Martin's archaic-sounding amendment of turncoat'. Two drifts: craven's 1400 is 14th-, not 15th-century, so '15th-century forms' overreaches for one of the three; and Adam Pulford is described on the page as working 'in marketing for Oxford Dictionaries', not as a lexicographer.

claims.claim: Hartinger calls the prose tight, clear and evocative and the individual chapter structure about as good as structure gets, faulting only scope.
claims.quote: about as good as structure gets

verdict.trueWording: The structure of the individual chapters is often about as good as structure gets
verdict.note: Quote verbatim; the prose limb is verbatim too, with the original's typo: 'He prose is tight and clear and evocative'. 'Faulting only scope' is a slight narrowing — his fault is that Martin 'seems to have lost complete control of his overall story' and traded story for 'atmosphere', of which length is one symptom. Post dated May 05, 2014, itself a repost of a 2012 piece.

claims.claim: The medieval-fantasy feel comes from the frequency of compounds rather than from any single coinage.

verdict.trueWording: derives not from a handful of obvious stock phrases
verdict.note: No quote was supplied, so verbatim status is not at issue. The 2013 post supports the cumulative-frequency argument twice: 'The more there are, the more frequently you encounter them on each page, the greater the sense of moving into his otherworld,' and the conclusion, where the medieval-fantasy sense 'derives not from a handful of obvious stock phrases, but from Martin's deep and systematic deployment of a carefully filtered... Anglo-Saxon vocabulary.' Two calibrations: the post's stated contrast is systematic Anglo-Saxon vocabulary versus stock phrases, not compounds versus 'any single coinage'; and compounds are explicitly 'just one of the verbal techniques.' The word 'cumulative' does not appear on this page (it appears in the 2014 post's conclusion).

claims.claim: He repeats a small set of words within a passage (cool, still) to build stillness and mood.
claims.quote: repetitions in this passage – of 'cool' and 'still'

verdict.trueWording: repetitions in this passage – of 'cool' and 'still'
verdict.note: Quotation is exact (en dash and curly quotes as printed). CAVEAT ON THE CLAIM, not the quote: the source explicitly refuses to settle the purpose the claim asserts — 'I can't decide whether the repetitions in this passage... are signs of haste, or careful repetitions designed to evoke the lazy, torpid atmosphere of Lord Martell's sea retreat.' The claim's 'to build stillness and mood' states as fact one of two alternatives the author leaves open, and the source's word is 'lazy, torpid atmosphere,' not stillness. Treat the purposive reading as the citing author's inference.

claims.claim: Confrontations are carried by short, charged exchanges that deliver the revelations rather than by narration.
claims.quote: terse, charged dialogue

verdict.trueWording: Confrontations between opposing characters are done though terse, charged dialogue
verdict.note: Exact match under heading '4 Dramatic dialogue' (the source's 'though' for 'through' is its own typo, outside the quoted span). 'Deliver the revelations' is supported: 'you experience a real dramatic shock when you realise, along with one character, the implications of another one's words.' The contrastive 'rather than by narration' is the citing author's framing; the page does not state that contrast.

claims.claim: An evaluative adverb in narration ('Stupidly, Jon argued') fuses narrator judgment with the character's own.
claims.quote: Stupidly, Jon argued

verdict.trueWording: Stupidly, Jon argued.
verdict.note: Exact match, quoted from AGOT: 'Stupidly, Jon argued. "I'll be fifteen on my name day," he said.' CAVEAT ON THE CLAIM: the essay poses this as an open question rather than asserting fusion — its lead-in is 'In this next quote, who thinks Jon is being stupid? Jon, or the narrator?' — and files it under 'Martin does not always control psychic distance.' 'Fuses narrator judgment with the character's own' is the citing author's resolution of an ambiguity the source deliberately leaves standing.

claims.claim: Words such as pug-nosed, longshoreman (1811), condone (1857), yen, burp, and snark leak modern English into Westeros.
claims.quote: shows you the seams of his work

verdict.trueWording: Martin shows you the seams of his work
verdict.note: Quotation appears word for word, in the snark passage: 'by using it in the exact same context, Martin shows you the seams of his work.' All six items check out: pug ('are there pugs in Westeros?', 'She was pug-nosed and bouncy'); 'Longshoreman came into English in 1811, according to Etymonline.com' (1811 exact); condone tied to 'the Matrimonial Causes Act, an 1857 piece of legislation' (1857 exact); yen 'is in fact about a hundred years old'; burp 'Only a few decades older than Martin' (charted 1932). Two precision notes: 1857 is the Act's date, the essay's explanation for the word taking hold in English, not an etymological first-use date; and snark is presented as a Lewis Carroll coinage rather than as modern English generally.

claims.claim: Many sentences are modular and deletable: a 1,897-word passage compresses to 427 words using only topic sentences.
claims.quote: modular sentences that can snap together like LEGO

verdict.trueWording: modular sentences that can snap together like LEGO
verdict.note: Quotation appears word for word. The figures are exact: 'Those seven paragraphs, totalling 427 words, are actually built from the first sentences of 26 different paragraphs, totalling 1,897 words.' Deletability is the essay's opening thesis: 'you can pull out quite a few sentences before they start getting wobbly.' Two directional notes: the essay assembled 427 words out of 1,897 rather than compressing a continuous passage, and the LEGO line is one of several speculative explanations ('Maybe... Or this is an epiphenomenon... Maybe it's...'), not an asserted finding.

claims.claim: Frequent single-sentence paragraphs sustain narrative momentum.
claims.quote: Martin has a fair number of one-lines

verdict.trueWording: (Martin has a fair number of one-lines.)
verdict.note: Quotation appears word for word, parenthetically. The momentum link is present but weaker than the claim states: the essay is hunting 'something beyond the plot that's contributing to the series' propulsiveness,' then offers 'Or this is an epiphenomenon, and the real driver is a short average paragraph. (Martin has a fair number of one-lines.)' So one-line paragraphs are floated as a possible driver among alternatives, and 'a fair number' is a softer quantity than the claim's 'Frequent'.

claims.claim: In A Game of Thrones semicolons and colons are used interchangeably (three on one page), a habit corrected by A Dance with Dragons.
claims.quote: he's gotten the semicolon figured out by now

verdict.trueWording: Seems like he's gotten the semicolon figured out by now
verdict.note: Quotation appears word for word. Opening sentence: 'In AGOT, Martin uses semicolons and colons interchangeably.' The page count is exact: 'Incredibly, there are three examples of this on one page, 239 in my edition of AGOT.' One softening the claim drops: the ADWD verdict is hedged and evidentially weak in the source, 'Seems like he's gotten the semicolon figured out by now, though, ADWD didn't pop any for me' - an absence of noticed instances by one reader, not a demonstrated correction.

claims.feature: purple register for nature and violence
claims.claim: The tone swings from casual to purple, with ornate diction reserved for wilderness (green) and bloodshed (red).
claims.source: At Sea Journal (Erik Germani), 'Purple Prose in Green and Red'
claims.quote: the tone can be very casual and very purple

verdict.trueWording: In ASOIAF, the tone can be very casual and very purple
verdict.note: Quotation appears word for word. The green/red framing is explicit: 'Here I'd like to point out Martin's reasons for using it: as an ecstatic response to nature and violence' and 'It's about the green and the red, for Martin.' Ornate diction is identified in the wilderness passage: 'Martin shifts into antiquated diction: "tangle of root and thorn and grasping limb"; "Knew not"; "small wonder".' Minor overstatement in the claim: the essay gives nature and violence as Martin's reasons for the high register, not as an exclusive reservation, and adds a second function - the register can 'capture the experience or distance the reader from it.'

claims.claim: Combat passages personify the sword and stretch or stop time.
claims.source: At Sea Journal (Erik Germani), 'Purple Prose in Green and Red'
claims.quote: time slept when swords woke

verdict.trueWording: It might have been minutes or it might have been hours; time slept when swords woke
verdict.note: Quotation appears word for word. Time distortion is directly supported by that sentence and its lead-in, 'Jaime could not have said how long he pressed the attack.' Weapon animation is present in the combat material the essay quotes: 'the longsword alive in his hands', 'The swords kissed and sprang apart and kissed again', and 'the gilded sword that had sipped the blood of the last of the Dragonkings'. One attribution note: 'personify' is the claimant's analytic label, not the essayist's word; the essay makes its explicit self-animation point about axes in the wilderness passage ('He doesn't tell us who is swinging these few axes, they seem to swing themselves, as though enchanted').

claims.claim: Backstory is delivered as monologue dressed as dialogue, assigned to talkative characters as a trait, lampshaded, or reported in summary rather than quoted.
claims.source: At Sea Journal (Erik Germani), 'Now, As We All Know'
claims.quote: It is a flashback dressed up as a monologue

verdict.trueWording: It is a flashback dressed up as a monologue
verdict.note: Quotation appears word for word, following Ned's roughly 650-word remembrance to Robert. All four mechanisms are confirmed. Trait assignment: 'Telling Catelyn stuff she already knows is Rodrik's thing... It's just a character trait!' and Hal Mollen, 'He had a penchant for loudly announcing the obvious.' Lampshading: 'Winking at the audience while doing something gauche (hanging a lampshade, as TvTropes would have it).' Summary over quotation: 'Sam Tarly's backstory feels better in comparison to the above, because Martin reports it instead of quoting directly.' One wording note: the claim inverts the essay's phrase - the source says flashback dressed up as a monologue, not monologue dressed as dialogue.

claims.claim: Chapters cycle among coercion, negotiation, action, travel, revelation, predicament, and disclosure scenes, each shoehorning in secondary information.
claims.quote: The narrative cycles between these types of scene.

verdict.trueWording: The narrative cycles between these types of scene.
verdict.note: Quotation appears word for word. Six of the seven types map directly to the essay's numbered list: coercion (1), 'Discussions/arguments about what to do/bargaining' (2), 'Action sequence' (3), 'Travelling sequence' (4), 'A predicament is sketched out' (6), 'Present information is disclosed' (7). The shoehorning half is explicit: 'Every chapter is like this. There is some central action to the scene, but Martin takes the opportunity to shoehorn in some other information.' One relabel to flag: the claim's 'revelation' stands for type 5, which the essay words as 'An enigma is laid out or an action is promised' - closer to a mystery posed or a promise made than to a revelation delivered.

claims.claim: Martin describes fantasy's proper language as dreamlike and defined by taste, colour, and texture.
claims.source: George R. R. Martin, 'On Fantasy' (1996), georgerrmartin.com
claims.quote: The best fantasy is written in the language of dreams.

verdict.trueWording: The best fantasy is written in the language of dreams.
verdict.note: Opening line of the essay, exact. Colour and taste are explicit in the following paragraph ("silver and scarlet, indigo and azure"; "Fantasy tastes of habaneros and honey"); "texture" is the analyst's inference from the material imagery ("obsidian veined with gold", "plywood and plastic"), not Martin's word.

claims.claim: He frames the reader's motive as recovering vividness of colour, which underwrites his heraldic and food description.
claims.source: George R. R. Martin, 'On Fantasy' (1996), georgerrmartin.com
claims.quote: We read fantasy to find the colors again

verdict.trueWording: We read fantasy to find the colors again, I think.
verdict.note: Exact (US spelling "colors" on the page). The reader-motive half is fully supported, and food/taste is present ("To taste strong spices"). The clause "underwrites his heraldic ... description" is the analyst's application; heraldry appears nowhere in the essay.

claims.claim: Chapters typically open with the character already eating, fighting, or mid-conversation.
claims.source: W.A. Hughes, 'How to Write a Chapter of ASOIAF', 2014-05-12 (satire)

verdict.trueWording: Start In The Middle of the Action
verdict.note: No quotation supplied. Step 2 lists "a) eating b) excreting c) fucking d) fighting or e) in the middle of a conversation". Slight overreach: the page scopes this to a character's first appearance and "within two pages", not to every chapter opening, and omits two of its five items.

claims.claim: Characters fixate on stock expressions in italics, which the satirist reads as padding.
claims.source: W.A. Hughes, 'How to Write a Chapter of ASOIAF', 2014-05-12 (satire)
claims.quote: isn't worth a mummer's fart

verdict.trueWording: someone in every chapter should find a way to exclaim that something "isn't worth a mummer's fart"
verdict.note: Quotation exact, but it sits in Step 4 (word choice), while the italics-and-padding point is Step 3: "recurring ideas or phrases they can't get out of their head... smashing through that word count". The claim fuses two separate steps; both halves are on the page, the linkage is the analyst's.

claims.claim: Setting facts are folded into ordinary exposition rather than explained.
claims.source: Jon Auerbach, 'Writing advice from the first chapter', 2017
claims.quote: the ninth year of summer, and the seventh of Bran's life

verdict.trueWording: It was the ninth year of summer, and the seventh of Bran's life.
verdict.note: Quotation exact. Support for the craft claim is indirect: the post reacts with a joke ("apparently the ninth year of summer on whatever crazy planet") rather than naming embedded worldbuilding; the nearest explicit statement is about Ice - "a good detail that G.R.R.M. tucks in here when readers won't be able to grasp its significance."

claims.claim: Backstory enters when a remark prompts the POV character's memory rather than by narrator summary.
claims.source: Dark Jackel's Howl, 'Let's Read AGOT Part 1', 2015-08-19
claims.quote: some character makes a comment or observation, which prompts memories

verdict.trueWording: "some character makes a comment or observation, which prompts memories and reactions from the POV character, Will"
verdict.note: Exact substring. 'rather than by narrator summary' is the claim's gloss on the page's "it's pretty minimalist" framing of the expositional style.

claims.claim: The prologue builds dread through negative sensory statements and dialogue with double meanings.
claims.source: The Fantasy Review, 'Prologue Summary and Analysis', 2023-10-14
claims.quote: The Others made no sound

verdict.trueWording: "The Others made no sound."
verdict.note: Word for word, but as the post's epigraph excerpt from the novel (with "The woods gave no answer"), not as the blogger's own analysis. The 'double meanings' half IS the page's analysis: the opening exchange is "clever wordplay" that on reread is "telling you to be very, very afraid of the dead". The page never uses the phrase 'negative sensory statements'.

claims.claim: Earlier physical detail (Bran's gargoyle handholds) is re-used as an instrument of later violence.
claims.source: Race for the Iron Throne (Steven Attewell), Bran VII ACOK, 2016-04-07
claims.quote: His tongue felt strange and thick in his mouth

verdict.trueWording: "the gargoyles that were Bran's handholds transformed into murder weapons"
verdict.note: The supplied quote "His tongue felt strange and thick in his mouth" IS on the page word for word, but it is a block quote about Bran's warging and does NOT evidence this claim. The claim's actual support is the separate sentence given as trueWording, which the claim calls "deliberate and thorough" callback. Quote/claim are mispaired.

claims.claim: A repeated phrase in a doomed POV ('the bloody snow') carries foreshadowing the character cannot read.
claims.source: Race for the Iron Throne (Steven Attewell), ASOS Prologue, 2016-04-18

verdict.trueWording: "GRRM loves a cheap pun, Chett's downfall is caused by snow"
verdict.note: The doomed-POV foreshadowing the character cannot read is supported. But 'refrain' overstates: the page carries "the bloody snow" once as its epigraph and once inside the quoted Chett passage; it never calls it a repeated phrase or refrain.

claims.claim: Jaime's italic commentary goes silent immediately before a violent act, forcing the reader to register it.
claims.quote: absolutely SILENT

verdict.trueWording: "jaime's smart-mouthed inner voice is absolutely SILENT about his feelings about brienne"
verdict.note: Exact, capitalisation included. 'forcing the reader to register it' is supported: "he wants that jolt, he wants to shake you. he wants you to NOTICE." Caveat: the page says 'inner voice'/'inner commentary'/'inner snarkbot', never 'italic'; and the silence runs through the Ronnet Connington exchange, with Jaime's golden hand striking him at the end.

claims.claim: 'Nuncle' and similar archaisms (pease, neeps) appear only from A Feast for Crows onward, a deliberate late shift some readers dislike.
claims.quote: It's totally an AFFC and onward thing

verdict.trueWording: "But it's totally an AFFC and onward thing, with GRRM deliberately archaic-ing his language (to many people's annoyance)"
verdict.note: Exact substring, and the dislike is the blogger's own (tag: "i am not a great fan of the archaic-ing of asoiaf"). Caveat: only 'nuncle' is dated to AFFC-onward. 'pease' and 'neeps' appear in a different post as "Other GRRM-style words from archaic English" with no book range attached, so the claim's parenthetical extends the source.

claims.claim: Text-mining across four series finds Martin uses -ly adverbs least and reads at about age ten by readability index.
claims.source: Winter Is Coming (Dan Selcke) on Dimitris Spathis, 2015-09-24
claims.quote: George R.R. Martin hates adverbs

verdict.trueWording: What does this chart tell us? That George R.R. Martin hates adverbs.
verdict.note: Quote exact. Four series confirmed (LOTR, Harry Potter, Hunger Games, ASOIAF) and 'you only need to be 10 years old to understand A Song of Ice and Fire'. Caveat: the page never says '-ly' adverbs nor the word 'least' - it credits an adverb chart hosted on Spathis' own Medium post.

claims.claim: Meal descriptions mark inclusion, class, and culture, with sensory verbs carrying the emotion.

verdict.trueWording: uses food to establish the emotional states of his characters
verdict.note: No quote was supplied. Belonging/class confirmed ('a sign of brotherhood, of the sense of fraternity'; Jon as bastard 'not fit to sit in the main hall'), culture confirmed ('Dothraki food, drink, and the way they celebrate tell us quite a bit about them as a group'). 'Sensory verbs' is the analyst's gloss, not the page's wording. Byline note: page credits 'By Andrea Guzman' in the body under poster Isabel Carrasco, translated by Oliver G. Alvar; date April 9 2019 matches.

claims.claim: The chronicler attributes the war's poetic name to some singer, the chronicle's habit of assigning romance to song and sobriety to record.
claims.source: George R.R. Martin, 'The Princess and the Queen' excerpt (primary text), Reactor/Tor.com

claims.page: Dangerous Women: The Princess and The Queen (Excerpt)
